title: OpenAI Jalapeno Custom AI ASIC at Hot Chips 2026
gist: At Hot Chips 2026, OpenAI detailed Jalapeno, an in-house inference ASIC built with Broadcom that went from initial RTL to tapeout in roughly nine months, and showed power-normalized benchmarks claiming Pareto-frontier leads over NVIDIA GB200/GB300 at 700W vs 1.2-1.4kW. The design was accelerated by OpenAI's own AI models in both hardware design (56% PPA win on a BF16 multiply) and kernel optimization (1.5-1.8x over expert-written kernels), and is framed as Gen 1 of a multi-generation roadmap.

insights.claim: OpenAI took its Jalapeno inference ASIC, co-built with Broadcom, from initial RTL to tapeout in roughly nine months — architecture concept in late 2024, RTL freeze in 2025, tapeout in late 2025, Codex running on silicon in early 2026, and ChatGPT on the chip shortly after.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Custom AI silicon cycles compressing to under a year erodes the moat of merchant GPU vendors and validates Broadcom's custom-ASIC franchise.
insights.quote: the chip’s roughly nine-month path from initial RTL to tapeout
insights.locator: OpenAI took the Hot Chips 2026 stage

insights.claim: OpenAI ran three third-party models (GPT-OSS, DeepSeek R1, 1T-parameter Kimi K2.5) on Jalapeno between A0 silicon return and the Hot Chips presentation, with none of them co-designed for the chip — evidence of software-stack generality and bring-up velocity.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Fast bring-up on non-native models undercuts the argument that in-house ASICs are locked to one workload; watch for other labs following.
insights.locator: OpenAI ran GPT-OSS to stress latency

insights.claim: OpenAI describes its chip-design execution as continuous convergence — the spec was not fully known up front but converged through a measure, verify, learn, change, repeat loop spanning workload simulation, RTL, QoR analysis, DV and physical design, with major changes landing up to the day of RTL freeze.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Iterative, AI-assisted spec convergence is a repeatable methodology other hyperscalers can copy, threatening incumbent EDA/design-services economics.
insights.quote: the specification converges through the design loop rather than being fully known up front

insights.claim: Celestica is named alongside Broadcom as a partner in OpenAI's Jalapeno program, tying the contract manufacturer into the custom AI-ASIC supply chain.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Confirms Celestica exposure to OpenAI custom-silicon rack builds — a revenue vector outside the NVIDIA ecosystem.
insights.quote: They also give a shout-out to Broadcom and Celestica.
insights.locator: They also give a shout-out

themes.theme: Power-normalized benchmarks vs NVIDIA and AMD

insights.claim: OpenAI benchmarks Jalapeno using SemiAnalysis InferenceX, a public power-normalized suite, with runs normalized to package TDP: Jalapeno at 700W versus NVIDIA GB200 at 1.2kW and GB300 and AMD MI355X at 1.4kW, measured against the July 2026 Pareto frontier of accelerators.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Power-normalized public benchmarking shifts the competitive metric from raw FLOPs to tokens-per-joule — the axis where custom ASICs beat merchant GPUs.
insights.locator: For comparisons, OpenAI uses InferenceX

insights.claim: On GPT-OSS 120B, Jalapeno at 700W holds the throughput-per-kilowatt Pareto frontier against the 1,200W GB200, with about 1.9x higher peak mixed tokens/sec/kW, roughly 1.7x lower end-to-end latency, and about 53.7x more throughput at the previous best time-between-tokens.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: If replicated, ~2x efficiency at nearly half the power directly attacks NVIDIA inference TCO; the 50x+ figures at prior-best latency show custom silicon opening new low-latency operating points GPUs cannot reach.
insights.locator: At matched operating points on GPT-OSS

insights.claim: On DeepSeek R1 670B in MXFP4, Jalapeno's matched-operating-point lead over the GB300 widens to about 1.7x peak mixed tokens/kW/sec, 3.6x lower end-to-end latency, and roughly 104.3x more throughput at the previous best time-between-tokens.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Gains widening at larger model scale suggests the architecture advantage compounds where inference spend concentrates — frontier-scale MoE serving.
insights.locator: On DeepSeek R1, the matched-operating-point

insights.claim: Even with Jalapeno handicapped in single-token mode against a GB300 running multi-token speculative decoding on DeepSeek R1, it still leads with about 1.5x higher peak mixed-token rate per kilowatt and 2.2x lower end-to-end latency.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The handicapped comparison is the credibility test — the lead surviving without speculative decoding implies a genuine hardware-efficiency edge, not a benchmark artifact.
insights.locator: OpenAI also runs Jalapeño in single-token

insights.claim: On the 1-trillion-parameter Kimi K2.5, Jalapeno at 700W beats the 1,400W GB300 with about 1.5x higher peak mixed tokens/sec/kW, 3.4x lower end-to-end latency, and roughly 56.1x higher throughput than the previous best time-between-tokens.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Demonstrates the chip scales to trillion-parameter multi-device serving — the workload class driving the largest inference capex.
insights.locator: Kimi K2.5 shows the largest relative

insights.claim: OpenAI claims sub-millisecond token-to-token latency on frontier models at economical throughputs, and says adding multi-token prediction would deliver a further 3x to 5x latency improvement at iso-efficiency — meaning the published numbers understate headroom.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Sub-ms TBT enables agentic and real-time products that are uneconomical on GPUs; the unclaimed MTP headroom is a signal the Gen 1 gap could widen further in software alone.
insights.quote: sub-millisecond token-to-token latency on frontier models at economical throughputs
insights.locator: OpenAI also claims sub-millisecond token-to-token

insights.claim: OpenAI's headline comparisons pit single-token Jalapeno against NVIDIA baselines using multi-token prediction, where MTP's seven draft-model turns plus one batched trunk pass can cut expensive large-model passes by up to 8x — a methodological asymmetry that actually favors the NVIDIA side in most charts.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Understanding the benchmark asymmetry matters when handicapping vendor claims — here the asymmetry runs against OpenAI, strengthening rather than weakening its numbers.
insights.locator: Jalapeño uses single-token prediction, whereas

insights.claim: OpenAI evaluates inference systems on two metrics — time to last token for user experience and tokens per joule for efficiency — comparing along the full Pareto frontier of request latency versus energy per token, explicitly rejecting chip counts, per-chip throughput, and time-to-first-token as the yardsticks.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for judging all inference-hardware claims; vendors optimizing TTFT or chip-level throughput may be optimizing the wrong axis as buyers converge on tokens-per-joule.
insights.quote: time to last token for user experience and tokens per joule for inference efficiency
insights.locator: OpenAI frames the design around two

insights.claim: OpenAI argues a single inference request spans three distinct hardware regimes — compute-bound prefill, ultra-low-batch latency-sensitive draft speculation, and memory-bandwidth-bound spec-verify decode with bursty MoE communication — so efficiency only counts if the whole request meets its end-to-end latency target.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This three-regime model explains why point-optimized accelerators disappoint in production and is the analytical frame for evaluating disaggregated-inference startups.
insights.locator: Moving into the architecture, OpenAI argues

insights.claim: OpenAI contends specialized heterogeneous inference fleets (separate prefill/decode hardware) are structurally inefficient because shifting workload mixes leave idle accelerators drawing baseline package, HBM, I/O and network power; Jalapeno instead uses one balanced chip that gates unused blocks per phase.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Directly against the popular prefill/decode disaggregation thesis — negative read-through for architectures and startups betting on heterogeneous specialized fleets.
insights.quote: idle accelerators still draw baseline power
insights.locator: Workload mixes shift the balance among

insights.claim: OpenAI's key system choice was keeping KV cache local on-chip and varying the active silicon mix of compute, memory and network per phase, rather than moving KV state across a network at every phase boundary between specialized systems.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: KV-locality vs KV-movement is the fault line in inference system design; bets on KV-transport interconnect and memory-pooling plays face pressure if the balanced-chip camp wins.
insights.quote: whether KV cache state moves between specialized systems or whether the active silicon mix changes within a single chip
insights.locator: This system-level design decision comes down

insights.claim: Despite a 128-chip aggregate HBM4 bandwidth above one petabyte per second implying 1,000-2,000 tokens/sec/user without speculative decoding (5,000-10,000 with it), OpenAI concedes the real system lands well below either rate — raw memory bandwidth is not the binding constraint on inference.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Cuts against the 'inference is purely HBM-bandwidth-bound' consensus that underpins some memory-supplier theses; latency architecture, not bandwidth, is the frontier.
insights.quote: indicating that raw bandwidth is not the only limiting resource
insights.locator: Jalapeño’s raw HBM4 bandwidth is striking

insights.claim: Jalapeno pairs each core slice with its own HBM slice for a fast local memory view and adds a specialized low-latency collective network for common cross-core patterns, keeping a general NoC only for non-critical traffic — attacking the long-latency paths, contended unified memory, and global memory fences that leave compute idle.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Locality-first memory architecture is the mechanism behind the latency wins; expect this pattern to spread across next-gen inference ASICs.
insights.locator: This architecture responds by pairing each

insights.claim: Jalapeno delivers 13.4 PFLOP/s of mxfp4 matrix compute, 15.4 TB/s of HBM4 bandwidth across 216 GiB in a 700W package, scaling to 27 EFLOP/s and 432 TiB across a 2,048-chip system.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Hard spec baseline for modeling OpenAI inference economics and for handicapping HBM4 demand outside NVIDIA/AMD sockets.
insights.locator: Jalapeño delivers 13.4 PFLOP/s of

insights.claim: The Jalapeno fabric uses a local 128-ASIC low-latency domain at 600 GB/s and a global 2,048-chip domain at 200 GB/s built as a half-flattened two-level Clos on Broadcom Tomahawk6 switches, with higher bandwidth reserved for tensor parallelism and lower for expert parallelism.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: OpenAI scale-out running on Broadcom Ethernet switching rather than NVLink/InfiniBand is a concrete design win for Broadcom networking and a negative read for NVIDIA's fabric attach rate.
insights.locator: A local Jalapeño domain reaches 128

themes.theme: AI designing and programming the chip

insights.claim: OpenAI used an internal AI model plus the XLS hardware description language in the Jalapeno flow, landing major changes up to the day of RTL freeze and beating a human baseline on measured PPA — including 56 percent on a back-to-back BF16 multiply alongside a 10 percent smaller matrix-unit area.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Quantified proof that AI-assisted RTL beats human design on PPA — a disruptive signal for EDA vendors and a productivity multiplier for every custom-silicon program.
insights.quote: 56 percent on a BF16 multiply, back-to-back with a 10 percent smaller matrix unit area
insights.locator: OpenAI used its own internal AI

insights.claim: Jalapeno's spatial programming model (each physical core programmed as a thread block via the Gluon framework, with explicit tensor placement and communication) was deliberately built to be simple for humans and easy for frontier AI to program, so AI search handles mapping, placement, scheduling and pipelining.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Designing hardware for AI programmers rather than human ones neutralizes the CUDA software-moat argument — the moat matters less if models, not people, write the kernels.
insights.quote: built to be simple for humans and easy for frontier AI to program
insights.locator: Jalapeño’s programming model is built to

insights.claim: Starting from functionally correct kernels, OpenAI's internal AI system drives optimization to the point that its attention and MoE kernels run 1.5x to 1.8x faster than existing expert-written implementations, validated end-to-end on-chip.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: AI-generated kernels beating experts collapses the software-ecosystem disadvantage that historically killed non-NVIDIA accelerators.
insights.quote: 1.5x to 1.8x faster than existing expert-written implementations, validated end-to-end on-chip
insights.locator: Starting from functionally correct kernels, an

insights.claim: Jalapeno is explicitly Gen 1 of a multi-generation OpenAI silicon roadmap: Gen 2 targets better performance per watt and Gen 3 aims at economical low-latency serving by unlocking aggregate HBM bandwidth rather than simply adding raw bandwidth.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A committed multi-gen roadmap means OpenAI's ASIC volume with Broadcom is structural, not a one-off experiment — durable share shift away from merchant GPUs for OpenAI inference.
insights.locator: OpenAI frames Jalapeño as Gen 1

insights.claim: Kennedy's takeaway is that a nine-month in-house ASIC demonstrates AI compressing hardware product cycles themselves, and that Jalapeno is a proof point encouraging other companies to attempt their own chip design.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: If AI-compressed design cycles generalize, expect a wave of new custom-silicon entrants — bullish design-partner and foundry volume, bearish for any single vendor's pricing power.
insights.quote: Building an in-house ASIC in about 9 months is wild.
insights.locator: Final Words
